chapters.title: Chapter One: The Basement
paragraphs: Burgundy had been awake for thirty-one hours.
He could tell by the count blinking in the corner of his monitor, the timer he set to motivate himself. The number didn't bother him. The shake in his right hand did.

The basement smelled like smoking copper. Three monitors glowed green-on-black in front of him, lines of code scrolling so fast they made the dim room flicker. Cables ran along the floor in bundles thicker than his arm, taped down with whatever he'd had on hand: duct tape, electrical tape, in one place a strip of his own shirt. Against the far wall, beneath a tarp, the prototype waited.
He hadn't looked at it in six hours. That was on purpose. If he looked he'd find something to fix, and he didn't have time to fix anything else. Tomorrow was the day.

Three monitors glowed in front of him: torque curve on the left, strain-gauge table in the middle, and on the right a text editor open on a function he had named GO. On the third line from the top there was an off-by-one error he had been looking at for almost an hour without seeing.

He saw it now. He pressed the tab key. He pressed it again. He pressed it a third time and committed the fix and ran the simulation again and watched the torque curve resolve into something less ugly than it had been.
He let out a breath. An eye twitched.

Above him, somewhere, the palace was quiet. The palace was always quiet at this hour. Even the kitchens, which started before dawn, had not yet started. Burgundy could hear the boiler in the next sublevel, a low irregular cough that had been part of the basement's soundtrack for so long that he no longer heard it unless he listened. He listened for a moment. Then he stopped listening and pressed his hands against his eyes and counted to ten.
He had been working on this thing for two years. This project no one understood. That he himself sometimes didn't understand.

Two years. Or, that was the official count. The number he gave himself when he was being honest about the project as a project. The truth was he had been working on something like the prototype for almost a decade, since he was eight years old, when he had taken apart the desk clock in the receiving room and put it back together upside down on purpose to see if his father would notice. His father had not noticed for two months. When he had noticed, he had cuffed Burgundy on the side of the head and told him to leave the clock alone. Burgundy had taken it apart again that night and put it back the right way, and his father had never mentioned it again.
He thought, sometimes, about the miners. The people the planet ran on.  Their faces, stained black, their dying lungs.  This whole world relied on their work.

He did not know any of them. He could not have. He was the prince, and the prince did not go into the mines except to stand at the rim during inspections, in the embroidered coat his father made him wear, while the foremen read from their clipboards and the King nodded at whatever they said and the miners below in the pits, black-faced, soaked through, holding their picks at their sides like rifles at parade, looked up at him without expression.

He had been to the rim of the South 12 Shaft three times in his life. It was the "worst" mine. It wasn't just a pit, but a deep labyrinth of tunnels. Burgundy's grandpa's had inspectors who  found some special vein of ore down there. "Never ending" is the how it was talked about. So they just kept digging down. for decades now. It had become infamous for how deep it went. A tangle of tunnels no single person knew the extent of. The elevators to get down to the deepest parts took 30 minutes one way. Or so Burgundy heard from his uncle who used to sneak out as a teenager and explore.

Burgundy only knew the surface of South 12 but remembered the smell. He remembered the way the work lights along the walls made the air look like it was full of something solid. He remembered one miner, a woman working a stretch of rock near the surface, swinging her pick, the working the stubborn rock with a chisel and hammer,  directing the black crumbs that came off that wall into an impossibly old cart. Her sweat seemed permanent.

He thought about her, sometimes. A lot, actually.  In fact the entire thing he was building in this basement, a robot with a drill attached,  could trace back to her.  A machine that could replace that woman.

He had not told anyone this. He was aware that it was the sort of thing that would sound stupid if he said it out loud, I built it for a woman whose name I do not know, and he was aware that this was also possibly true.
His father did not know about the basement.
Or, Burgundy hoped his father did not know about the basement. It was possible that he did.
His father was the King of Dross, a small planet that was packed with valuable ores.

"Our ores make travel between the stars possible" is something his Father would say at the dinner table at least one a month. Whoever sat at the table heard it: Burgundy, a visiting dignitary, a governor, a minister. Burgundy didn't really understand what it meant. He never asked.
The tribute ships came every month and he had watched them for as long as he could stand at a window. Massive cargo vessels descending onto the planet to collect.
When he was very small he had asked his father what they loaded into the massive vessels. what were they taking away from our planet. Everything, his father had said. He didn't explain.

He had learned, eventually, the name of the man whose ships these were. He had never met the man. Nobody on Dross had ever met the man. Nicholas was a name his father said the way other people talked about the season's rainfall, as a fact of the world that determined abundance or scarcity. It was all Nicholas.

The basement where he now worked had been a wine cellar once, before some great-great-uncle had decided wine was beneath royal dignity. The bottles had been carried up and broken in the courtyard.  Burgundy had read about this in one of the old palace histories,  He had taken the cellar over when he was twelve. He had run the cables down himself, through a vent shaft he had widened with a drill over a long summer.  Everything else he had scavenged: a motor left to rust in the eastern yard, ball bearings from a broken serving cart, copper wire he stripped from a wall no one had lit in years. Scrap was easy to come by and would carry it down a piece at a time, at night.
And then he would work. Not for anyone. For himself.
He had told himself, sometimes, that he was preparing for something.
He had not been sure, until tonight, what.
Burgundy finished wiring up the robot's arm. He toggled his controllers to test it out. fluid and smooth. this was working. It would be impressive tomorrow.
He had been careful in his rehearsals not to imagine his father's response.
His mother had given him a glance, at dinner earlier.
That was all. A glance. She had not said anything to him during the meal. She rarely did, when his father was present.

But at one point, when the King had been talking to one of his ministers about the southern tariff and Burgundy had been pushing food around his plate, she had looked at him across the table, briefly, and then looked away.

That night they were joined by the finance minister, The governor of the northern fields, down from the iron country for the season's accounting, the master of the eastern works, who laughed at the King's jokes half a beat before they finished. Two security men whose names Burgundy had never been offered. Three of the men had brought wives, and the wives wore dresses that had crossed systems to reach Dross. They spoke endlessly about things and people Burgundy did not know or have any interest in.  the southern tariff was raised, weighed, and settled in the mild tones men use when the argument has already happened somewhere else. His father spoke last on it, briefly. The minister nodded. The governor nodded.

And exactly then, his mother shot him that look again. She was trying to get his attention.  Or was she? He had spent his whole life noticing the things she did not say and trying to assemble them, and he had never quite managed it. Sometimes he thought she watched him the way you watch a clock you have built yourself, waiting to see whether it will keep time. Sometimes he thought she did not watch him at all and he was inventing it.
He was probably inventing it.

The code terminal blipped. The torque simulation had finished and produced an output graph he stared at for almost a minute before he understood what he was looking at. The graph was fine. The graph had been fine the last three times he had run it. He was running the simulation because he could not think of anything else to do, and he could not think of anything else to do because he was very tired.
He looked at his hand. Still shaking
He looked at the timer in the corner of the monitor. The number had ticked over to thirty-two hours.
He thought, I should sleep.
He thought, I cannot sleep.
The boiler coughed below.
Somewhere far above him, the palace clock struck three.
He laid his head down on his arms.

He told himself it was only for a moment. He told himself he just needed his eyes to stop hurting. He told himself a few more things, small reasonable things, and then, between one of those things and the next, he was no longer telling himself anything at all.

The basement was dark and green and full of small mechanical noise, and somewhere far above the palace, the planet kept turning toward the day he had spent two years preparing for, the day he had no way of knowing would not go the way he had rehearsed.

chapters.title: Chapter Two: The Court
paragraphs: The Hall of Light was the most used room in the castle. It's where all the decisions were made, mostly during morning council hour

It was not a beautiful space. The King had spent his money  elsewhere like the approach to the palace, rebuilt to be twenty lanes wide and flanked with carved stone giants of Burgundy's ancestors; or the stables, rebuilt twice, stocked with beasts from other systems; there was a private hunting ground that had required the forced removal of three villages, eighteen hundred people forced to relocate so the king could hunt once a year.

The hall itself had a huge arched ceiling, its stone ribs fanning out from the tops of the columns, and was mostly empty.  The walls were the same grey stone as the floor.  Down the center of the long hall ran a single pale path, the stone worn a shade lighter by the feet of everyone who had ever  walked from the huge entrance door to back side of the hall where the throne sat, atop a dais three steps up.

The hall did have one thing worth looking at. Behind the King's throne, a massive window ran nearly floor to ceiling. A thousand small panes of colored glass, and set among them, thin cut sheets of translucent stone, the rare kind pulled from Dross's mines. In daylight the stone panes would catch the sunlight and split it into gleaming threads of colored light in a way no glass ever could.  And at night the stone glowed faint and pale like embers.

The window was the work of one of Burgundy's great-grandfathers, a king who had been obsessed with the stars. He had taken his cosmology from the Ghai, the ancient underground people who had lived here for a thousand years before Burgundy's clan conquered. He built the window based on their reading of the sky: every pane placed so that the sun, moving through the seasons, would strike certain stones on certain days. Each alignment meant something. The light on one stone marked the turning of the year; on another, a planting; on another, the harvest. When Burgundy was eleven, a tutor had stood him in the hall and explained the whole system, pane by pane.
Burgundy remembered none of it.
On this particular morning, the one he had been preparing for for years Burgundy had not planned to arrive late.

He had planned to wake at five, with an hour to wash and rehearse the pitch one more time and walk the prototype up the spiral stair without anyone seeing him. He had not planned to wake at seven, sleeve print on his face, the hours-counter showing thirty-five, his neck stiff in a way he could already tell would last all day.

As he rushed to wash his face in the basement basin, he looked over at the robot as it booted up. In the thin morning light it looked smaller than it did at night. It stood on its one fat wheel, chest-high, the salvaged frame bolted and rewelded until the seams showed like scars on its round metal chest and torso with two arms. One for grabbing, and one for drilling rock. The cutting bit at the drill arm's end was ground down to a dull working shine. Low on the front of the robot was a green-glass panel, where his code lived. The brain of the thing positioned where the heart would live. This morning the panel pulsing a slow green pulse, indicating "active", and Burgundy looked at it whole for the first time in six hours and thought, before he could stop himself, that it was either the best thing he had ever made or a toy, and that in a few hours his father would decide which.

The doors of the receiving hall were never open during the council hour. He had been walking past them his whole life. He had never walked through them at this hour. But today he did pushing open the great doors and walking in accompanied by a short robot on a single fat wheel that was proving to be quite loud against the stone.

He had not noticed in the basement how loud it was. Down there the ventilation hum had absorbed the sound; up here as he walked the path of worn stone from the door to the throne, the wheel sounded like someone dragging a coin across a slate.

The boy and his robot walked toward the throne. His father sat at the far end, flanked by the long dark council tables filled with rows of advisors and stacked paper. The council was on a break. Advisors talked among themselves, heir voices an echoing hum in the huge hall.
And behind them, the morning light was blaring through the great glass window, splashing colorful light across the floors and walls of the otherwise grey room.
As Burgundy got closer he caught a clear sight of his father on the throne talking to his security minister.

The King a large man.  Broad through the chest, a serious expression etched onto his brow, his hair going silver at the temples. He wore a golden band around his head, set with inlays of Dross's most exotic minerals (HELP FROM JUNE RINGS LLC FOR JEWELRY DESCRIPTOR PLZ. #TagSTAICE #wutzURStatice )
When Burgundy had been very small he had thought his father was the largest thing in the world. He still thought so sometimes in dreams.

His mother stood beside the throne. Mira's hair was dust-grey, and she wore a gown the color of dried blood. She did not smile when she saw her son. Burgundy felt her watching him . He searched her face for the look she had given him at dinner the night before. He could not find it. She was looking at him a different way now. A tense unchanging expressions.

As he arrived at the foot of the Dais, the group started to go silent and look. The advisors stared,  Burgundy snuck a glance of their confused expressions,  the one on the right had a smear of ink on his white collar he did not know was there. The one on the left looked at the prototype briefly and then away.
Burgundy's heart was ramping up.
"Ah yes, Burgundy." Thundered the King's voice into the newly silent room, "You asked to see me,"
"Yes, sir."
"You know this is the council hour"
"I know, sir."
"Then I assume you have something worth the council's time. What is that?" his eye shooting to the robot.

Burgundy stepped forward and so did the Robot, The wheel was loud again. Then it parked and lit up, the panel on its chest pulsed green, ready for the demonstration. It made a soft sound, almost like clearing its throat.
"Father," he said. "I want to show you something."
That was not what he had planned to say.  But the words came out anyway, and the prototype was already glowing, and there was no taking it back, so he kept going.

"It mines," he said. "Or it will, in the fields. Twice as fast as a man with a pick. Maybe more, with proper tuning. I built it from scrap. The components cost less than a month's pay for a single miner. If we built a hundred —"
"Stop."
The King had not raised his voice. He did not need to.
"Father can I —"
"I said stop."
Burgundy stopped.

The hall was very quiet.  The hall was fully silent for the first time since Burgundy had entered it.  The advisors were looking at the floor. Mira was looking at Burgundy. The King was looking at the prototype.
"What do you imagine you have built?" the King asked.
"A miner. A better one."
"And what do you imagine I will do with it?"
"Whatever you want. Make more, put them in the mines. I mean you're the King. You could —"
"I am the King. Yes" His father said it gently, almost patiently, "And do you understand what that means?"
"It means —"
"It means I rule. I rule this planet. A planet whose ores make star travel possible." He smiled a charming smile, and looked around, he was going into a familiar script of his, Burgundy could see it.
"But actually you know what? I don't actually rule this planet. I don't rule Ore. Do you know what I actually Rule?"
Then a pause. Long than was comfortable.
"Men."

He said it softly, the punch line to his well-rehearsed performance. He was smiling broadly now "I rule men. I do not need to mine the mines faster. My job is to rule the men who mine them. Do you understand the difference?"
Burgundy did not answer. His throat was too tight.
The King stood.

He was tall, and he came down the three steps slowly, his robe whispering as they brushed against the stone, and he stopped in front of the robot. He looked at it for a long time. He did not touch it.
Then he looked at his son.

"You think I haven't seen this before," he said. "You think you're the first person to bring a clever invention to our throne? There have been a hundred of you. Every one of them believed he had discovered the thing that would change our world. Make our lives better. Do you know what changes the world, Burgundy?"
"What."

The word came out smaller than he had wanted. He’d anticipated his father asking rhetorical questions and had practiced responses with some level dignity. But here, now, with the wheel silent and the green panel pulsing and his father an arm's length away and Mira's eyes burning into him, the word what came out the way it had come out of him at eight years old, holding a clock he had taken apart wrong.
"Willingness" the King said. "Willingness to do what it takes to to keep order and peace. That's what we do here."
His voice was almost kind.

"You are my son. You will rule one day. Ruling isn't just sitting on this throne with this gold band around your head. It's a craft. Our craft. It is not learned by playing with robots. It is learned at my side. And you have not been at my side. You have been hiding in the dark, playing with wires, while I have been ruling. What I have given you is the future of this kingdom. And you bring me this?"
He kicked the prototype.

It was not a hard kick,  the prototype rocked back on its single fat wheel, and the green panel flickered, and somewhere along the right side of the hall one of the advisors made a small soft sound that might have been a laugh and might have been a cough.
Burgundy heard it.

In the basement, in the long hours of the night, he had run every scenario he could imagine for how this conversation might go. He had imagined the yes. He had imagined the no.  He had been careful, he remembered now being careful, not to imagine a laugh. He had not been able to bring himself to imagine a laugh.
But the laugh had not come from his father.

The laugh, or the cough, he would never know which, had come from an old man with ink on his collar, an old man whose name Burgundy was not sure he had ever known, an old man who had been standing in this room since before Burgundy was born.
"Take it away," the King said.
"Father —"

"Take it away, Burgundy. Do not bring it back. Do not bring me anything like it again. The next time I see you in this hall I want to see you in council robes. Listening. Learning. Not in overalls. Not with grease on your hands. Do you understand me?"
Burgundy looked down at the prototype.
"Yes, sir," he said.
He did not look at Mira.
He did not look at the advisors.

He turned the prototype around, by hand, because he did not trust himself to give it a command in a voice that would not crack, and he pushed it back toward the doors. The wheel with the loud sound again as it moves across twenty colorful shades of sunlight. The hall behind him silent.  Burgundy walked the length of the hall with his hands on the prototype's housing, and at the doors he did not stop, and he did not look back, and he pushed through into the corridor.
The doors closed behind him.
He stood for a moment with his hand on the prototype, in the long cold corridor where his footsteps would have echoed if he had taken any. He stood very still. Shaking to himself
The prototype hummed beside him. Its green panel pulsed once, gently.

chapters.title: chapter 3 Mira's Wing
paragraphs: Through the closed doors, the council resumed. His father's voice was a low rumble without shape. An advisor answered. Then his father again, longer, and something in it must have been a joke, because it got its soft, polite laughs.
He was still listening when the small side door in the corridor  opened.
His mother slipped out.

She did not look at him. She closed the door behind her without a sound. She stood for a moment with her hand still on the handle, listening to the council, until the King said something else that was answered by the same polite noise, and then she turned to Burgundy, and she put one finger against her lips.
"Come," she whispered. It was less a word than a breath. "Bring it." her eyes dashing to the robot.
Burgundy opened his mouth.
She shook her head, a single small motion, and turned, and began to walk down the corridor.
He put his hand on the prototype's housing. He pressed the small command that told it to follow. The prototype rolled after him.
They walked.

They took a corridor Burgundy knew, the long one that led past the council chamber toward the eastern courtyards. Then Mira turned right, into a smaller corridor that Burgundy had only walked twice in his life. And from here he began to lose his bearings.
She took him past a door he had believed was a broom closet. Behind the door was a narrow flight of stairs going up.
She started up them without hesitation.

Burgundy stopped at the foot of them. The prototype stopped behind him. Its wheel, a single fat wheel, salvaged from a serving cart, rated for stone floors and stone floors only, was going to have to descend stairs.
He had prepared for this, sort of.

Two months ago, in the basement, he had cut the wheel open. He had lined the inner rim with a rubber sleeve. He then wired a small air compressor into the chest cavity. He had coded a 'soft-mode' that would let the tire release air, enough for the wheel to deform around the edges of steps so it could climb them.

It had worked decently this morning as he took the robot up a few small sets of stairs from the basement to the council. But he had never taken it up a full spiral flight. He had not been sure he would ever need to.
He pressed the command.

The prototype's chest made a small hydraulic sound. The wheel visibly relaxed,  it looked, for a moment, as though it had lost some air. Then Burgundy pushed it against the first step. The wheel deformed. It caught. He pushed. The prototype rocked forward, awkward like it was about to fall, but then it mounted the first step, and then the second, and then a rhythm settled into it that was almost a walk. It was climbing.
Mira was five steps up, watching.
"You really built this?" she asked quietly
"Yes."
She nodded once and kept climbing.

The stone at the top of the stairs was a different color, warmer, cream instead of grey, and the sconces along the walls were made of a metal he could not immediately identify, worked with a pattern that looked, when he looked closely, like nothing he had seen anywhere else in the palace. The pattern was intricate and repeating.  The air smelled different too. Not the wet-stone smell of the palace's lower halls. It smelled like books.
Mira did not stop to let him look.

She took him through a small entry hall, and into a larger corridor with a high vaulted ceiling and windows on one side, all shuttered, all dusty. Their shoes made no sound; the floor here was carpeted, a long red runner going grey. Burgundy realized, walking down it, that the runner had not been walked on nearly it all. It felt brand new.
"Mother, where —"
"Not yet."

They passed doors. Most were closed. One was open a crack, and through it Burgundy caught a glimpse of a sitting room, chairs still angled toward each other, but otherwise empty and gathering dust. The whole wing had the feeling of a play that had been rehearsed once and then never performed.
They turned a corner. They turned another.
Mira stopped at a set of double doors, pushed them open, and stepped through into a room that stopped him where he stood.

Burgundy had known there was a library in the palace. There were several. The one near the entrance, where his father sometimes met with foreign envoys, had a wall of leather-bound treaties and a globe that had not been updated in his lifetime. The one off the council chamber held the ledgers and the tax records and the tribute receipts. Neither of them was this.
This library was three stories tall and another two stories down, dug deep into the ground, all contained in this one massive room.

the room was cut up into an intricate labyrinth of bookcases and crossings, stacks running into stacks, with narrow iron walkways bridging the gaps at each level so a person could walk from one wall of books to another without ever touching the floor.  There were ladders on brass rails that traveled the length of each wall. And doors. Many little arched doors,  tucked into the bookshelves at no noticeable pattern. There was a spiral staircase in the center that connected the whole thing. down below at the basement level were tables, long, dark, oiled tables, with reading lamps and stacked books and, on one of them, a small model of a star system Burgundy did not recognize. There was a whole corner of maps and globes. There were, so far as he could see at a glance, tens of thousands of books, and looking at the shelf to his left he could see some up close noticing that half of them were not in any language he had been taught to read.
He stopped. Awed by this huge space he hadn't known about.
The prototype rolled up beside him and stopped too, its wheel humming back to solid mode, its soft-mode air-cycle finishing with a small sigh.
Mira let him look for a moment. Then he asked, "Mother, what is this place?"
She said, without turning:
"This is my library. This whole wing is mine. built at my request when I agreed to marry your father. My mother sent most of these books. This is a piece of my family"
"Your family," Burgundy said.
She turned.
For the first time since the corridor she smiled, a small, thin smile.
"Yes," she said. "My family."

She crossed to a shelf on the eastern wall and climbed the ladder without hurry, and Burgundy followed her up because he did not know what else to do, and the robot waited below on its wheel, its green panel pulsing slowly in the low light. At the top of the ladder Mira walked along the gallery to a specific shelf and stopped in front of it.
The books on the shelf were mostly grey and brown. A few had gold lettering.
One was yellow.
She reached up and put her hand on the yellow book, a plain yellow, no title on the spine, and she looked at Burgundy.
"This," she said, "was your grandfather's."
Then she pulled.

The book came out an inch, then stopped. Something inside the shelf clicked, a small mechanical sound, quiet but precise, and the whole bookcase shifted on some hidden hinge and began to swing inward, silently, like a great door on very old bearings.
Behind the bookcase was another room.

chapters.title: chapter 4 -The White Room
paragraphs: The room behind the bookcase was white.

Actually gleaming white. The walls were paneled in some smooth pale material that was not stone and not wood and not metal exactly. Overhead, no oil lamps, no hanging bulbs, a row of long flat panels shed a clean cold light Burgundy had seen only once before

When he was young, Mira would take him to watch the royal engineers design the planet’s mining machinery. He’d sit for hours if she let him, watching the engineers bent over their drafting tables with rulers and stacks of papers nearly as tall as he was. The engineers worked under rows of long flat panels that shed a bright cold light on their work.

The secret room he was now looking at had that light, that feeling. Even the same smell. The tables were clean. They were laid out with equipment. Not scrap. Not salvage. Real equipment: sealed processors in their original packaging, still bearing manufacturer's marks.; oscilloscopes newer than anything the palace had bought in his lifetime; a small array of green-glass panels stacked between wooden dividers; toolboxes with drawers labeled in a fine hand he recognized, after a moment, as his mother's.

Against the back wall stood a low shelf of documents: folders, ledgers, thin bound reports, all with the same neat spine tags. A stack of manifests. A stack of star charts. A stack of what looked, from where Burgundy stood, like schematics.
She walked to the nearest table and set her hand on it lightly.
"Come in," she said.

He walked to the first table. He picked up a processor. He turned it over. It was a model he had read about in a manual two years old and had never expected to see in his own hand. This one unit was certainly worth more than a year of a miner's pay. There were twelve of them on this table alone.
He set it back down. His hand was shaking again, though not from tiredness this time.
"Mother," he said.
"Yes."
"What is this room? This Library?"

Mira crossed to a chair near one of the tables and sat down. She sat the way she sat at council, straight-backed, hands folded, but her face was different than it was at council. For the first time Burgundy could remember, she looked like a person and not like a queen.
"Your father does not know about this room, and it must stay that way" she said. "That is the first thing to understand."
"All right."
"Nobody in your father's line has ever known about this room and a few other rooms I have in my wing. These are only known to my family"
"Your family?" Burgundy said again, because he still did not understand what she meant when she said it.
She looked at him.
"Sit down," she said.
He sat.
"You know that I was not from here," she said. "You know that your father married me as part of a bargain between families But the version you've been told leaves things out ."
"What does it leave out?"
She considered the question.

"My family," she said, "is not a family in the way your father's family is. There is no title. There is no throne. There is no country. There is only a network. The network is very old and very large and it is spread across nine systems that I know of and possibly more. It moves things. We, move things. Some of those things are legal in some places. Many of them are not legal anywhere. And a large portion of what we move, and what has kept us in business for the last two centuries, is minerals. Specifically the sort of minerals that come from inside this planet, minerals you can't find anywhere else in this part of the galaxy. Minerals that fuel advanced technology like the processors in your hand."
Burgundy looked down at his hand. He had picked the processor up again without meaning to.

"Dross is not important to the Core-world Alliance. We're too far away, too small. But Dross is very important to us. To my family. We move a great deal of what Dross produces. Not through the tribute channels, those are Nicholas's. He takes most. Has for decades. My family picks up the rest. It moves and trades the minerals from this planet, finding whatever buyer will take them, and not asking too many questions about their end use.
She paused.
"Dross has been informally trading with our people for years," she said,  but it was always full of mistrust. Occasional conflicts, because well, my people aren't just traders. They also raid."
"Raid?"
"They find ships carrying cargo in remote parts of the system and raid them. Take them for ransom, or they pillage and sell the cargo"
"So they're pirates?" Burgundy said.

"Yes, you could say that." Burgundy could tell she didn't like the label.  She continued, "Your father's father wanted to formalize trade ties with my family, and my family offered a solution. The solution was a marriage, an alliance built on trade and trust. The marriage was me."
Burgundy could not think of anything to say.
"I was seventeen," Mira said

"I didn't have much of a choice, I was young, and even though I was on a path to study in the Core world academies, your grandfather wanted me for his son. That was the deal. I was the family bargaining chip, every generation has one. I knew I had to be sent here to this place. So I asked for the library. I asked for a whole wing to be built so I could continue my studies.  I wanted it to be big and grand. I had dreams of opening my own academy here. To help modernize this place.  My family agreed to fund the wing. Your father's family agreed to build it.

"For the last 19 years I've been procuring books and technology from the far away systems, using my family's smuggling routes. Every cargo vessel that comes to collect Dross minerals carries a second, hidden manifest, the things I've requested. My cousin runs the family's Dross trade. She has been very helpful."
"What about the academy?"
Mira laughed a resentful gutteral laugh

"Your father would never let it happen. I didn’t know that in the beginning. I was hopeful. Naive, even. But he put a stop to it before it could even begin. He shut it down from the very beginning. Said I could have my books and my wing and my studies but that was to be kept to myself."
Then Silence. Burgundy tried to hold all of it at once and could not.

His mother was a pirate. Not the daughter of some distant royal house, the way he had always been told. Her family ran a cartel, raiders and smugglers who moved black-market cargo across at least nine systems. Though in a way, he thought, that made her royalty after all. Any family that controlled that much trade would command more wealth than most thrones.

And here she stood, the sacrificial bride to secure black market minerals, now surrounded by machines and parts Burgundy hadn't known existed. All of it smuggled onto the planet under her husband's nose.
Burgundy had spent two years believing the basement was the one big secret in the house. But there had been two secrets, and his was the smaller one.
"How does Father not know about any of this?"
"He believes that what I do here is read books. He has not been in this wing since three weeks after our marriage. He has never opened the door to this library. He is not curious."
She said the last word — curious — with something like tenderness. It was the first tender thing Burgundy had heard her say all morning.
"Why?" said Burgundy, looking at his mother as if for the first time.
"Why what?"
"Why buy all of this?"

"Because I am curious. I always have been, about the galaxy, about the way gadgets and inventions like this can feel like magic. My grandfather lived through the invention of interstellar travel, and when I was a girl he would tell me how it changed everything. Whole systems pulled out of poverty in a generation, because suddenly they could trade with the core world across the stars."
There was a pause. Then Mira said:

"So I have been collecting. and secretly seeding knowledge into this planet. A disc slipped into a servant's basket now and then, carried down to the quarters where someone might read it. A better pump sent to a village that had been hauling water by hand. Small things, quietly, for years." She looked at him. "The people of this planet believe they are poor because the galaxy made them poor. They do not know they have been cut off from it on purpose."
Burgundy did not know how to answer.
"I decided a month ago that I was going to show you this room. Because I've been watching you in the basement"
"You know about the basement?"
"I have known about the basement for more than a year, Burgundy. I've said nothing because I wanted to see how far you would take it on your own."
Burgundy said nothing.
"You brought it to him today" She continued, "your robot. I knew you would. And I guessed the outcome. I told myself that if your father rejects it, it would be time to show you this."
They stood in silence. She walked to one of the tables. and picked up a spool of fine-gauge wire and turned it over in her fingers, once, and set it back down where it had been.
"I am going to offer you a bargain," she said. "Listen carefully. I am going to offer it once."
"All right."

"This room is yours. Everything in it. The parts, the tech. The tools.  Whatever else you need, tell me, and I will get it from anywhere in the system. Even from the Core worlds I can get the most up to date discs and even a fair number of parts.  You will not have to sneak scrap out of the southern shaft anymore.  You will build here, in this room, with real materials. I have already collected discs with some of the most up to date research. And here, you will build whatever you want to build."
She looked at him.
"In exchange," she said, "you will be the prince your father wants."
He looked at her.

"You will show up to council every morning, You will wear the coat. You will listen.  You will visit the mines with your father when he goes, and you will nod when he speaks, and you will smile the way he wants you to smile. You will be seen at the tribute inspections. You will attend the seasonal meeting with regional governors.  You will travel to the docks each month with him to see the tribute shipment goes smoothly. You will be, in every public detail, the son he wanted to have. If he calls on you to speak, you will speak, and you will say what he wants to hear. "
"He'll never believe it," Burgundy said.

"He will," Mira said. "He will believe it because he wants to. That is the thing about your father you have not yet understood. He does not see what is in front of him. He sees what he expects. Give him what he expects, and he will not look further. He will believe that the lecture he gave you after he shut down your robot created a change of heart and that you've grown up, just like he always knew you would."
Burgundy sat with his hands in his lap. He did not look at the processors on the table. He looked at his mother.
"You are asking me to become him," he said.

"I am asking you to look like him. just to keep his eyes away from what you are doing here. if he finds out about this room, it will end very poorly for all of us <<<I need to raise the stakes of him finding out. Hint to how bad it would be.
"Do we have a bargain?"
He thought about it.

He thought about his father kicking the prototype. He thought about the small sound the advisor with ink on his collar had made, the sound that might have been a laugh. He thought about the woman in the South 12 Shaft who had not looked up at him. He thought about the tribute ships coming down each month.
He thought about his father saying I rule men.
"Yes," he said. "We have a bargain."

They stood in silence, Burgundy's mind racing as he saw his mother, or some version of his mother, for the first time. And so much started to make sense. the stories she would tell about inventors and gadgets that connected the stars, the errands she would take him to visit the royal engineer. How he would find tools and gadgets on his shelf. In his toy bin. He realized that this moment wasn't random. This was by design. This was his mother's design.
She crossed the room and picked up something from the far table, a small object he could not see clearly until she brought it to him, and she pressed it into his hand.
It was a tiny processor unit. Not the one he had picked up first. A shinier, newer looking one with fine gold lines worked across its surface.
"Begin," she said. and left.

chapters.title: chapter 5 Double Life
paragraphs: TODO: >>>>>>>>>Weave in the imagery of the big colorful window and keep establishing the Hall of Light as a key setting.

From that morning on, Burgundy began living two lives. Protocol ruled one. Sunlight streaming through stained glass windows in the grand hall making sweat drip down his embroidered coat as he performed his expected role. The other took place after dusk, behind a nondescript yellow book high up on a shelf.

Burgundy threw himself into being the perfect prince, but the work took a toll. He felt it grind him down. A dull ache behind his eyes always after a day of it.  It was during the quiet hours working in the secret bright white room surrounded by possibilities that renewed him.
the months went on and neither life knew about the other, and Burgundy carried an increasing fear that his father was on to him.

but the more time passed  the more he realized Mira was right.  His father seemed to believe nothing was amiss. That the lecture had worked. The days he spent in the light of the colorful window, by his father's side, he realized that the King saw the son he expected to see, the boy finally bent into shape, and he did not look further. Burgundy watched his father not look further, morning after morning, and filed it away.
He listened.
That was the thing about council that surprised him: how much there was to actually learn, once he stopped resenting the room.
He learned the tribute.

He had known about Nicholas his whole life but more like a child knows a fairytale. Now he learned the mechanics. The arrangement was old, older than his father, older than his grandfather. Nicholas provided security. That was the word the ministers used, security, always without irony, and it took Burgundy three months of listening to understand everything the word contained. Dross sat in a remote, dangerous part of a remote system, months of hard travel from the lanes of the Core-word Alliance. The Alliance's markets were distant; its protection was theoretical. A planet full of minerals with no fleet of its own was like warehouse of valuables with the doors unlocked. Nicholas kept the doors locked.

Nicholas's ships patrolled the approaches, and Nicholas's name, more than his ships, kept the raiders of six systems from descending onto Dross to pillage or conquer. In exchange, Nicholas took unrefined ore. 60% of what they produced. The royalty of Dross had resented the bargain for four generations and yet for four generations they had complied, because it worked, and because nothing else would. Every resource-rich planet in the region lived under some version of this arrangement. It was not an alliance. It was extortion with a schedule. The ministers did not call it that. Burgundy learned not to call it that either, out loud.
He learned the mines.

Not the rim-of-the-shaft version he had been shown as a child. The real accounting. Dross harvested eleven commercially significant minerals. Iron in bulk from the northern fields, where the seams ran shallow and wide. Copper and tin from the eastern hills. And from the deep shafts in the south,  the dangerous ones, the ones that took lives,  the specialty ores. These were rare, useful, valuable, and worth shipping across systems. Sense blue-black corvite, which was refined offworld and manufactured into every processor in the whole galaxy; threnite, which held a charge; and thin veins of antibarytic osmarine, the strangest substance on the planet, and the source of his fathers cliché. Osmarine was the reason ships could cross between star systems. Crews spotted it by the clean streak in a dirty wall: dust would not settle on it. Once refined, it did not sit in the hand; it rose, lazily, like a bubble, pressing up under the fingers. It weighed less than nothing. When it was discovered, fifty-three years ago, it changed everything. The core worlds learned to open doors in space, and it was osmarine — only osmarine — that could hold those doors open.
Dross was one of hundreds of worlds where it was found.

He learned prices. That a single crate of refined corvite was worth more than a year of the northern fields' iron harvest. He learned that the corvite in one of the processors on his mother's white tables had, in all likelihood, come out of the ground less than forty kilometers from where he sat. It was then likely shipped offworld raw, refined in some distant system's foundries, assembled into components and sold. Mostly the Core worlds, but also onto the shadow market, where it ended up in a white room 60 meters above the mines where the metal started.

Nobody on Dross could build a processor.  Other's controlled that, guarded it jealously. So Dross sold the flour and bought the bread, and this explained, finally, why his father was so aggressively averse to any kind of technological development on the planet.  Why his "craft" was ruling men to mine year in and year out.
He learned the army.

He had grown up thinking of the palace guard as the army. It was not. The army was three thousand men in barracks near the major shaft complexes, and it had not fought an external enemy in living memory, because external enemies were Nicholas's department. The army existed for domestic disputes. That was the ledger term: domestic disputes. It meant strikes. It meant slowdowns. It meant the year before Burgundy was born, when the southern shaft workers had refused to go down for eleven days and the army had gone into the workers' quarter and afterward the ledgers showed a one-time expense labeled pacification and repair. The army existed to keep the miners mining. Burgundy sat in council and watched his father review the army's budget with the same attention he gave the tribute, and understood that his father considered them the same expense.
He learned the festivals.

This was the lesson that stayed with him longest. Twice a year, at New Year's and at the midsummer Descent, the King opened the storehouses. Alcohol for every workers' quarter, paid from the royal accounts. Three days of suspended shifts. Music, lanterns, the great drum lines that Burgundy had heard from the palace walls his whole childhood, a low thunder rolling up from the city that he had always assumed was simply what joy sounded like.

The midsummer Descent, his tutors had told him, went back to the Ghai, the mining people who had ruled Dross before his father's line, who marked the longest day by descending together into the oldest shaft to hang lanterns for their dead, to sing and drum and chant a cathardic chant and refusing to bring up a single stone, then followed by two days of feasting and lamp-lit processions, and folk music and spirit worship. Their marriages would happen during this festival.

And under the King’s alcohol the Descent had an older fuel: something the elders drank from shallow cups that glowed faintly in the dark, a smell like hot metal and rain on road, passed hand to hand in the oldest rites.

Millions of people lived on Dross in conditions that anyone looking honestly would describe as slow grinding attrition, and twice a year the cities below the palace erupted into celebration so bright and loud it could be seen from orbit, and Burgundy had grown up believing this proved something about the spirit of the place.
It did prove something. He just had the something wrong.

He was at his father's side, eight months in, reviewing the festival provision, the King signing off on the alcohol allotments line by line, generous, unhurried, when his father said, without looking up:
"Do you know why I pay for this?"
"No, sir."

"Because a man who has something to look forward to does not burn down what he has." His father signed the last line. "Remember that. It is cheaper and more effective than the army, and it works better. Men do not rebel in the weeks before a festival. They do not rebel in the weeks after, while they are still telling stories about it. Time it right and you are never more than a few weeks from safety." He set down the pen. "That is the craft. Nobody will teach it to you honestly but me."
Burgundy nodded the way he had learned to nod.

Some days, that was the hardest part of the whole performance, not the pretending, but the learning. His father was a careful ruler. That was the thing Burgundy had not expected. The cruelty was not stupidity; it was, as his father always said "craft", refined over generations, applied with patience. The festivals, the army, the tribute, the shaved stipends. It all fit together, it all worked, and his father moved through it with the fluency of a man who had genuinely mastered his inheritance. Burgundy sat at his left hand and nodded and learned the craft of ruling men, and told himself he was learning it as reconnaissance, and was never fully sure this was true.
The nights belonged to the white room.
He found his own ways up. That was the first project. His mother's route through the broom-closet stair was hers; using it risked pattern, and pattern risked notice.

The palace's roots were deeper than its towers. Old dungeon galleries, drainage vaults, dead corridors sealed and forgotten by men who had died before his grandfather was born. And through his exploration he discovered that Mira's wing had  been built onto a disused arm of one of these subterranean  complexes, its foundations grafted into the old cells.
Over the first month he mapped three separate routes from the basement to his mother's wing, each surfacing through a different forgotten door.

In the white room, for the first few months, he read. And only read. He discovered that there was entire world of knowledge from the core worlds. The knowledge came on discs. And the discs, he came to understand, were the shape of the whole civilization.

There was no living connection between the stars. That was the fact underneath everything, the fact the Core World Alliance's own maps politely minimized: information could be beamed between worlds, but a signal was months crossing what a ship crossed in weeks, the signal decayed and stuttering by the time it arrival. So knowledge moved the way freight moved: in batches, on hulls. The great relay stations of the core worlds gathered transmissions the way harbors gather cargo, wrote them onto discs, and the discs rode out along the trade lanes toward the periphery. A disc was a slab of pressed crystal the size of Burgundy's palm, dense with more text than the palace's three libraries combined, and by the time one reached Dross the research on it was a year old at minimum, often three. It did not matter. On Dross, three years behind the core was still fifty years ahead of anything else on the planet.

Mira's cousin brought the discs in with the cargo runs They would come in a small wooden with divider slits and packed with wool and sawdust. In those first few months, Burgundy began to crave these discs. He would slip his mother a written list, folded into the book she was reading at breakfast, and two or three weeks later a crate would arrive in the white room with the discs pressed between wool packing, labeled in a language he had begun teaching himself. He could slip a disc into his terminal and start reading: journals of the core-world academies, engineering symposium collections, survey papers that mapped whole fields in a single sitting, patent filings by the thousand — each one a blueprint of somebody's solved problem — and the discipline he hunted for across all of them, the research on teaching code to drive a mechanical body.

He devoured all of it. He had no desire to build anything until he had absorbed what the core worlds had discovered in their academies, generations of advanced knowledge. What he found was despite his basic education, he could handle follow the papers, the research. He had been tinkering with eletronics since he was 8, reading engineering books (50 years old) since he was 11. His mind thirsted for this kind of information.

From his reading he understood that the cutting edge in the core worlds was the nexus of robotics and code. How to get a machine to not only obey a program, but how to get it to log feedback and write new code to improve itself. Everyone was talking about this. But it was clear that no one in the core worlds had been able to implement this idea into anything useful. It was still locked up in the minds and and labortories of academies and theoreticians.

He read papers on feedback architectures. He read papers on selection pressure applied to instruction sets, on programs bred like livestock across ten thousand generations in a single night, on the strange and apparently unresolved arguments about how far the technique could be pushed before the program's own goals drifted out from under its maker. Half the mathematics was beyond him. but with time he taught himself, disc by disc, working backward through citations, filling notebooks and becoming more aware than ever that he had a mind that locked in on hard things and did not let go. It wasn't easy, but it wasn't hard either.

chapters.title: chapter 6 Mira's Shipment
paragraphs: One night in the ninth month, the white room had to wait.
Mira came to his door after the palace had gone quiet. She knocked quietly. When he opened it she said only, "Wear something dark. Not the coat."
He did not ask.

They went down. She took a route he did not know, outside and through a gate in the north wall that a guard opened without looking at either of them, then along a path running east, toward low ground beyond the cargo field where the tribute loaded. Burgundy had assumed ships came down on Dross in exactly one place. He had been wrong about most things his mother touched.
There was a second field. Smaller. Lit only by amber lamps set low along its edges. A freighter sat on the landing pad, dark except for a few small utility lights no bigger than lamp-wicks.
This was not one of Nicholas's grey giants, which never landed at all. This was much smaller, maybe 10% the size. It was scuffed, patched, resting on wheels. Its cargo ramp was down.
Nobody hurried. That was the first thing he noticed. The loaders rolled crates up the ramp on low sleds.
Burgundy and Mira approached the ramp just as a woman was walking down it out of the ship to meet them. She was carrying a clipboard under her  arm.  Was this Ressa, his mother's cousin?

She held the slate out to Mira. "Manifest's ready. Ressa signed the outbound this afternoon.  The medicine order is short two pallets. The vendor's problem, not ours." So this wasn't Ressa, but rather one of her people.  His mother's cousin ran the trade without attending it. Then, with a glance at Burgundy that lasted no more than a half a second the woman said, "is this..."
"Yes" Mira said.
The woman snuck one more glance at burgundy then turned back up the ramp signaling to the loaders to proceed.
Mira began focusing on the papers on the clipboard, scanning each line and occasionally signing her name.
Burgundy watched the ship.

Up the ramp went the crates of ore. He knew it by the markings now: density codes, grade markings, black corvite in sealed bundles. And beside the ore, in a separate stack the crews handled differently, more slowly, in padded cradles: casks. Small. Banded with metal. When a loader tilted one to seat it on the sled, the seam of the lid showed a faint glow, cold and steady.

He knew what it was. He had heard the word over the years. Mostly in a whisper: Cinder. A mind altering drug. The substance that fueled the spiritual dimension of the midsummer Descent. Refined from a rare deep seam mineral called Cindrite in a method the Ghai discovered. Fleks of it were ground with the root of a stone weed and then consumed as a tea that glowed pale blue. Cinder was sacred in the old rites but illegal in every system. And yet there was a market for it throughout the whole galaxy. It was a stimulant that ran a man for two days and gave him blissful visions. This was Dross's second harvest, their cash crop, made of rock, now flowing up a ramp in casks bound for the black market run by his mother's family.

And down the ramp came the arriving cargo. Burgundy had expected the incoming cargo to be illicit items like drugs or weapons. But instead he saw seed stock in heavy sacks. Casks of cooking oil, sacks of grain marked in a language he couldn't read. The basics of a starving society.

And, at the end, a stack of boxes small and large that Burgundy recognized. , coils of special wire, servo assemblies nested in foam, a flat crate of carbon frame stock TKTKTKTKTKT MORE GEAR. small wooded boxes he knew contained with crystal discs from the core world, packed tightly between wool and sawdust.

It was worrisome to have it all out in the open like this. The crew carrying his secret down the ramp on dollys like any other shipment. But to them this was just another crate. It may look suspicious to his father, but His father didn't ever come to these shipments. Hadn't for years. He preferred Mira to be the interface.
Mira looked at one of the crew and said "Lew." and nodded her head at the bundle of Burgundy's items.
Lew must have been the insider that Mira paid to get all this from the cargo field to the white room behind the bookshelf. He had no idea what kind of arrangment they had but he trusted it was safe.
Lew gave almost no acknowledgment that he had heard but went straight to gather the boxes and crates onto a motorized loader, and off he went into the dark.

Mira was finishing on the clipboard now. She initialed a line. She stopped at another. "This count is wrong. there were only 17 casks." The woman on the ramp checked; agreed. Mira corrected it herself, small precise figures, the same hand that labeled the toolbox drawers in the white room.

chapters.title: chapter 7 DREKKO
paragraphs: The nights turned from studying discs to actually building.

The hardware changed everything. The processors from Mira's tables ran his feedback code four hundred times faster than the salvaged board in his first prototype; simulations that had taken a night now took a minute, which meant he could be wrong four hundred times as often. The crates brought hydraulics of a kind Dross's own industry had never seen,  sealed actuators, compact and strong enough to put three tons of pressure through a joint the size of his fist. They brought strain sensors finer than anything in the mines, servo assemblies, spun-carbon frame stock that weighed a third of the salvaged loader steel.

this made building easy by comparison. like putting together a puzzle. and By the end of the first year there were three prototypes of his drilling robot. he would call this generation 2 of a robot he was now calling "DREKKO".

They stood in a row along the white room's western wall, and they no longer looked like the machine his father had kicked. The single serving-cart wheel was gone; each unit now ran on a pair of independently driven treaded tracks that could soften or stiffen on command, his old sleeve-and-compressor trick, rebuilt with real components, so that the machines climbed the dungeon stairs behind him with a rocking, patient  easy gait. Each carried twin drill arms on hydraulic mounts, a cutting head he had ground himself from offworld tool-stock, a sorting bucket slung between the tracks. In their chests, behind green glass, the  advanced processors ran his code. He had rebuilt the feedback architecture three times from what the discs taught him. The machines scored their own work now, depth of cut, energy spent per kilogram, waste ratio.
They were, by any measure that had existed on Dross a year ago, marvels.

he would test the robots' ability to mine on a practice wall he found in the deepest room of his dungeon routes, an old cell gallery whose back wall, he had discovered in the second month. It was not built basic stone but of valuable mineral: the palace's foundations sat directly on the shoulder of the southern ore country, and somewhere in the centuries , when power shifted hand, the new ruler had built the palace atop an old mine. there was still unmined riches here. Burgundy had tested the rock out of habit, and the sensor mast had come back with a reading he made it repeat three times.
Corvite. A seam of it, thick at the room, running diagonally through the rock like a vein of night.

It was, he understood, a small fortune sitting inside the palace's own foundations, unmined because unmapped, unmapped because no one had ever thought to mine the dungeons. It was also, more usefully, the perfect teacher. Corvite was the hardest ore on Dross: dense, brittle in the wrong ways, prone to shattering into worthless gravel if the cutting angle was wrong by even a few degrees. The southern shafts lost more men to corvite seams than to any other work. If the machines could learn corvite, they could mine anything on the planet.

So every night, after council, after the coat came off, Burgundy went down through the old galleries and set the three prototypes against the wall, and watched them try. He moved his array of computers form teh white room to this dungeon-turned testing room so he could work down there and watch the robots try to cut into the rock

They were not failing, exactly. That was what made it hard. Each unit could bore into the seam. Each could strip freed ore into its bucket, sort waste rock by density, back out, and resume. Watching them work, a foreman from the southern shafts would have wept. three machines, no lungs to ruin, no stipends, no festivals required, chewing steadily into the hardest ore on the planet.

But The pace was wrong. He clocked them against the numbers he now knew from council: a good southern crew, twelve miners with picks and a blast allotment, pulled roughly a ton of raw corvite in a shift, losing a third of it to shatter. His three machines together managed perhaps half that, losing a quarter. Better per machine than a man. Not better enough. At this rate, replacing one shaft's crews would take three hundred machines, and he could build, with every disc and every crate and every stolen midnight hour, perhaps one every 90 days.

And they did not improve the way he needed them to.  they did not do whathe discs said they could with the right mix of code and hardware. and That was the true wall. His feedback code let each machine tune itself, a better angle here, a smarter torque curve there, but the tuning flattened out. Each prototype would improve for a week, ten days, and then settle onto a plateau, grinding away at the seam with a competence that never became mastery. He would adjust the scoring, and the machine would climb a little, and plateau again. and He  once again was the bottleneck. Every real improvement still ran through him: his diagnosis, his rewrite, his upload. Three machines waiting on one exhausted seventeen-year-old's judgment, and the seventeen-year-old was spending his days nodding at tribute ledgers.
18 months. Three machines, and a plateau he could not code his way past.

Some nights he sat on the cold floor of the gallery with his back against the old cell bars, the notebooks piled beside him, the green panels pulsing their patient rhythm against the dark, and did the arithmetic again, all the theoritical math the smartest minds in the galaxy had published promising code and hardware that would learn and grow like a human brain.  It never did. What he had built was remarkable. What he had built was insufficient. The distance between those two facts was where he lived now,  and he had begun to suspect, in the grey hours when the drum of the drills blurred into the sound of his own pulse, that no amount of his own cleverness would close the gap. He could not think fast enough to set these three machines free to think for themselves.

chapters.title: chapter 8 The Bridge
paragraphs: It began on a spring morning, 20 months after his mother first swung open the bookcase, and it began the way every important thing in Burgundy's life had begun: disguised as an ordinary day.

The day was worse than ordinary  in fact. It was mundane in the specific, grinding way that palace days could be mundane: a morning council about grain storage, a midday audience with a delegation of northern foremen whose grievance took two hours to state and one sentence to deny, an afternoon review of festival provisioning that his father conducted line by line, signature by signature, while the light moved slowly across the council chamber floor. Burgundy sat through all of it. He nodded in the right places. He had been nodding in the right places for almost 2 years now, and the nodding had become so automatic that he sometimes caught himself doing it alone, at night, at his workbench, agreeing with no one.
The whole day, one thought sat behind his eyes like a coal.
The discs.

His mother had passed him a new crate the week before, and this batch was different. He had known it was different by the third page of the first disc, read standing up, coat still on. For years the research he devoured had lived on one side of a canyon: software that could improve itself, code breeding code, selection pressure applied to instruction sets in clean simulated worlds. On the other side of the canyon stood his machines, real hardware, real rock, real dust clogging real joints.  A program could remake itself a thousand times a second, but it was still reasoning about a body it could not feel, in a world it could not touch, and so every real improvement still had to cross the canyon on Burgundy's back.
The new discs were about the bridge.

Core-world teams in top labs, three of them, working the same problem from different directions, their papers arriving on Dross pressed together on one crystal wafer, had begun closing the loop through the hardware itself.  producing experiments in a lab that showed real promise. The machine's own sensors feeding the machine's own learning, every strain gauge and thermal reading and torque curve pouring into the scoring functions in real time, like human senses to a human brain. The papers called it "closed-loop embodiment algorithms."

ANd the night before this spring day, Burgunday had read them all, three times each. and that's when it hit him The papers were brilliant but they were blind. Each team had proved the loop could close, in simulation, on a rig, in a world scrubbed clean of the things that made his machines choke, the real world. dust, heat, physics. and none of them, he saw, reading the same three authors argue past one another, had ever spent a night on their backs under a machine with sealant on their hands. They were so deeply confident in their controlled worlds that they missed that the hard, filthy, unglamorous work of making it survive contact with an actual world was beneath the math, or beyond it, or simply invisible to men who had never held a tool. And Burgundy, reading in a stolen room, on a backwater planet, with grease under his nails and years of failure, understood something that surprised him: He knew things they did not. He saw solutions that they could only argue about with vague words and concepts like "real world industrial application scenarios". He was...ahead of them.
He got back to the white room that evening before the lamps in the workers' quarter came on, and he worked.

he arrived with a new clarity on his problem, potentially the final frontier to making the robot teach itself:  the sensor buses on his prototypes had been built, by him, in a different life, to report their readings on a fixed cycle to a fixed log. The learning loop needed them raw and constant, a firehose instead of a faucet, a waterfall of real time data.  But every time he opened the data channels all the way, the processors drowned. The scoring functions fell behind the sensations they were supposed to score. The machines got clumsy, worse than before, drunk on their own feeling, and twice that night a drill arm slammed a cutting head into the corvite at an angle that sent shatter pinging off the gallery walls like shrapnel.
he had to replace a drill arm, twice that night something he had done 20 times by now.

He tried throttling the flow. He tried batching it. He tried letting the machine choose its own sampling rate, which the second paper hinted at and the third paper warned against, and the warning proved correct in a way that cost him a hydraulic line and an hour on his back under the second prototype with a mix of sealant and lubracant on his hands.

By the fourth hour of the night he had stopped being methodical. He knew he had stopped and he let it happen. There was a mode he went into, past a certain hour, that he did not entirely trust and could not entirely do without, where the experiments stopped being designed and started being thrown. He rewired the sensor buses on all three machines in three different configurations. He wrote four scoring variants and could no longer remember, by the end, which machine carried which. He gave them access  to the micro-charge dispensers he had mounted on their arms a month earlier, these were little explosives the size of beads, dispesed from magazines within the robots' arms. He had never used thembefore, they were meant for an experiment in pre-fracturing the rock, but he had shelved the idea as too dangerous to automate.  but tonight he was letting everything fly. He set bounds on the charges. He checked the bounds twice to make sure he wasn't about to blow up the whole foundation of the castle.

Then he lined the three prototypes up against the seam, barely scarred by two years of their patient, insufficient chewing, and he loaded the whole reckless suite of experiments into the queue, every variant, every configuration, set to run in rotation, each machine scoring itself and passing what it learned sideways to the other two.
He looked up, and the high thin slit window of the cell had was ilumnating with a warm sharp light.
Dawn. He had done it again. Council was in two hours and he had not slept in, he counted, twenty-six hours. He had to press go on this flurry of code and machinery and leave.
Wash, coat, council, foremen, docks. The tribute came down today.
He looked at the three machines idling against the black seam, their green panels pulsing, the experiment queue loaded and waiting on his word.
"Go," he said tio himself and pressed one button on his keyboard and left them working, as he often did.

He did not look back at the wall. If he had, there would have been nothing to see. It looked like every other morning he had left them: three patient machines, a barely wounded vein, a boy going up the old stairs two at a time with his coat over his arm.
Council was a blur

He got through the grain reports. He got through a dispute between two southern governors . Twice his head dipped, the full nod, chin to chest, and the second time he came back from it to find the room silent and his father looking at him down the length of the table.
"Am I boring you," the King said.
"No, sir. I apologize. I was reading late."
"Reading."
"The northern field reports." The lie arrived without being sent for. A year and a half of practice.
His father studied him a moment longer. "Read earlier," he said, and turned back to the table, and Burgundy exhaled through his nose, slowly, the way you let pressure out of a line.

The main business of the council was "groups." which was the royalty euphemism for gatherings of disgruntled citizens who were discussing strike or rebellion or anything of the sort.    There had been "groups" in the workers' quarters. Secret ones, at night, in the drying sheds and the pump rooms, the third such network broken up in a year. The word strike had been used; the interior minister said the word committee, which Burgundy had learned in almost two years of council was the word this room feared most. Six men had been taken. The minister recommended, and the King approved, that the taking be kept quiet, because with the festival five weeks out, quiet plus festival would bleed the pressure better than any public lesson.

"They are tired," the King said, signing. "Tired men make threats in sheds. Then the drums start and the drink is poured, and they remember they have something to lose, and they lose interest in losing it." he chuckled to himself. He set down the pen and looked, briefly, at his son, a teaching look, checking that the lesson had landed. Burgundy nodded

But something in his chest had leaned forward, listening, because there was something new in what the minister had said: six men taken, a third network in a year, the pressure rising faster than festivals could bleed it. And Burgundy filed the numbers away with all the other numbers, down in the dark where he kept them.

The tribute came down at midday, and Burgundy stood on the observation platform at his father's right hand and watched, as he had watched every month for almost two years, and it had never once stopped being the most alien thing he had ever seen.

From the platform, while they waited, the whole planet lay open around him. The sky was the pale hard white it always was, a sky the color of nothing, never fully blue and never fully dark, and under it the city climbed toward the palace in terraces of grey stone and rust roofing, hills of shanty towns barely held together, nests and webs of wires up and down the steep streets that followed no plan. On and one, until the city met a feeble strip of forest, one of the last bits of green on the whole planet. And from there,  the land opened into the pit country, the great open wounds of the southern shafts.

Nicholas's ships did not land. That was the first thing about them, the thing that reorganized your understanding of what a ship was. They arrived out of the white sky, three of them today, each the length of the palace and its grounds laid end to end, and they stopped, and hung, a hundred meters above the cargo field, without wings, without scaffolding, without any visible negotiation with gravity. Their hulls were the grey of deep water and utterly unmarked, and they made a sound that was less a sound than a pressure, a low field of force that Burgundy felt in his molars and in the bones of his chest, and that made the whole field of stacked crates, ten thousand tonnes of ore, graded, weighed, sealed, a month of the planet's blood in boxes, look like an offering laid out of fear. which is what it was.
Then the arms came down.

They unfolded from the bellies of the ships in silence, joint after joint after joint, white and precise, each one long enough to reach from the palace gate to the throne, and they began to pick up the crates. thirty-tonne crates rising in gentle clusters, drawn up into holds that never showed their insides. Nicolas's soldiers  stood on the field in their painted safety rings and watched, hard men with hooks on their belts.

⟦The platform behind them held the usual small court of the field: two regional governors in grey formal coats, the tribute master with his ledger men, a colonel of the domestic army standing where he could watch both the loading and the crowd that watched it. They stood at his father's shoulder with the ease of men who had stood there their whole lives. The ore was Dross's. The field, Burgundy understood without being told, belonged to them.⟧
Burgundy was so tired that the membrane between his two lives had gone thin, and the day-prince stood on the platform in his coat while the night-builder counted joints, estimated torque
He could not help it.

If those arms had a feedback loop, he thought, they would teach themselves to sort mid-air, to nest the ascending clusters tighter, to shave a second off every lift and then a second off the shaving. The thought belonged to the night. And behind it, because he was too tired to keep the two rooms separate, sat the machines he had left against the seam that morning, and the small bright hope that the explsoive had not brought the castle down on them.
His head dipped.

He caught it, half a second, no more, and came back to the pressure-hum and the white sky, and found his father looking at him. Not with anger. That was the strange thing. The King had seen the dip, and something in his face was almost soft.
"You're tired," the King said, quietly, under the hum.
"Yes, sir."
His father turned back to the field, to the last crates rising into the grey hulls, and he was silent for a while, and then he said, still watching the ships:

"You've become a great prince. I want you to know I see it. You'll be king someday, sooner than either of us would like, the way the years are going, and for the first time I believe you're ready for it. More than ready." He paused. The arms folded themselves away, joint after joint, into the bellies of the massive ships. "I'm glad you gave up those childish things. The toys, the wires. I know it wasn't easy, it never is, giving up what we love first. But look at you." He nodded at the field, at the order of it, at the month's blood rising into the sky on schedule. "This suits you. This is right for you. This is what you are."
The ships went up without seeming to move, the way the sun crosses a sky, and were gone, and the pressure lifted out of Burgundy's molars, and the field was just a field again, emptied.
"Thank you, Father," Burgundy said.
It was, he reflected, walking off the platform at his father's side, the kindest thing his father had ever said to him.

He was released from his duties an hour before dusk. by the time he reached the last of his three routes through the old galleries he was running, coat over his arm, taking the worn stairs down in the dark by memory.
He smelled it before he saw it.

Rock dust. In the hallway. thick. Not the ordinary haze the prototypes raised in a night's work, a thickness in the air of the hall of the old jail cells, a mineral fog that hung in the light of his lamp, and under it a smell he knew from exactly one place in his life: the rim of a working shaft. Blasting residue. Deep rock, opened.
He came around the last turn into the his cell-turned-lab and stopped.
The wall was gone.

Not damaged. Not advanced upon. Gone — where the seam had been, where almost two years of patient insufficient chewing had left a scarred black face, there was now a hole. A tunnel. Round-shouldered, clean-walled, taller than he was, driven straight into the living rock, and so deep that his lamp simply failed inside it, the light falling into the dark the way a stone falls into a well.
The three prototypes were not in the gallery.

Burgundy stood at the mouth of the tunnel for a long moment, listening to his own pulse beating on  hisneck, and then he did the thing that almost two years of discipline had built into him: he went to the terminal first.
The logs were still streaming.

He read standing up, then sitting, then leaning into the screen with both hands on the desk, scrolling, not breathing right.
